content: The process of authorizing new medicinal products ensures that medicines released for public use are thoroughly evaluated to meet international standards of quality, safety, and efficacy. This process also assesses whether the benefit-to-risk ratio of the medicine is favorable for its intended use. Regulatory authorities often conduct post-marketing surveillance and monitor adverse events associated with established interventions. While some national regulatory authorities (NRAs) are well-developed and comprehensive, others have limited capacity. NRAs play a critical role in the research environment, and for clinical trials to achieve their potential, NRAs must efficiently support trials using risk-based, proportionate approaches. In addition to NRAs and ethics committees, local institutional committees may sometimes require further clinical trial approval. The World Health Organization (WHO) Secretariat provides technical assistance to strengthen NRAs, including oversight of clinical trials. The WHO Global Benchmarking Tool offers a framework for Member States to improve the functioning of their NRAs. NRAs should act promptly, possess clinical trial review expertise, and maintain transparency regarding document submission requirements and timelines for trial approval. Procedures should be regularly reviewed, unnecessary bureaucracy eliminated, and processes adapted to changes in the clinical trial landscape. Not all clinical trials generate data for submission to NRAs. For example, trials focusing on behavioral interventions may not require marketing authorization. NRAs should only be involved in trials within their regulatory scope, as defined by local regulations. Ethical oversight is a fundamental aspect of health research, as reflected in WHO’s ethics guidance. Key reference documents for ethical clinical trial practices include the WMA Declaration of Helsinki, the WMA Declaration of Taipei, and the CIOMS International Ethical Guidelines. At the country level, local research ethics committees (RECs), also known as institutional review boards (IRBs), review all research involving human participants, including clinical trial proposals. RECs have the authority to approve, reject, or request modifications to trials and may suspend or terminate trials when necessary. RECs operate independently and include multidisciplinary members to ensure diverse perspectives, including community and societal viewpoints. The WHO Secretariat has developed tools to help Member States evaluate their capacity to provide ethical oversight for health-related research involving humans. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization has issued indicators for strengthening national research ethics systems and a tool for accrediting RECs. RECs should act efficiently, possess clinical trial review expertise, and maintain transparency regarding document submission requirements and timelines for trial approval. Procedures should be reviewed regularly, and unnecessary bureaucracy eliminated to adapt to changes in the clinical trial landscape. Interagency coordination and harmonization are essential for the efficient authorization of multicenter clinical trials. Systems such as parallel submissions to NRAs and RECs, reliance mechanisms, or joint reviews can reduce duplication while ensuring rigorous and timely authorization processes. WHO supports single REC models for multicenter trials and encourages regulatory harmonization and reliance on work performed by other regulators. Pooling expertise into a single national body can maximize resource use and improve trial efficiency. The European Union’s Clinical Trials Information System allows sponsors to apply for regulatory authorization in up to 30 countries through a single online application. Similarly, the Health Research Authority in England promotes coordinated research review across the UK through its Integrated Research Application System. In Africa, the African Vaccine Regulators Forum (AVAREF) provides a platform for coordinated review of multicountry clinical trial applications, supporting research and development while strengthening oversight capacity. The need for interagency harmonization has been highlighted by public health emergencies such as the HIV pandemic and outbreaks of Ebola and Zika virus diseases. WHO has published guidance on rapid research review during emergencies, and AVAREF has successfully implemented such models. For example, AVAREF’s emergency provisions were used for a large multicountry clinical trial in Africa involving 13 countries and multiple sponsors. Efficient, high-quality clinical trials require adequate infrastructure, including laboratories and clinical trial units (CTUs). Investment in sustainable laboratory facilities is critical, considering factors such as equipment costs, staffing, accreditation, and access to reference laboratories. Smaller CTUs often face challenges such as high staff turnover, short-term contracts, and limited opportunities for career progression, which can hinder their ability to participate in trials. There is a recognized need to shift from disease-specific CTUs to broad-based, disease-agnostic CTUs capable of addressing diverse research scenarios.
